Title: Storing Fresh Herbs

Fresh herbs like basil, cilantro, and parsley last noticeably longer when treated like
cut flowers rather than left loose in the crisper drawer. Trim about half an inch off
the stems at an angle, place them upright in a jar with roughly an inch of water, and
cover the leaves loosely with a plastic bag before refrigerating. This mimics the plant's
natural water uptake and slows wilting considerably compared to just wrapping them in a
paper towel.

Basil is a notable exception to this method. Unlike other herbs, basil is highly
sensitive to cold and will blacken and turn slimy within a day or two in the fridge.
Instead, keep basil in the same jar-of-water setup but leave it at room temperature,
away from direct sunlight, and it will often keep for a week or more, sometimes even
growing small roots.

For herbs you won't use within a week regardless of method, freezing is a reliable
backup — chop them and freeze in ice cube trays with a little olive oil or water, then
pop out cubes as needed for cooking.

Title: Substituting Baking Powder for Baking Soda

Baking soda is a single-acting leavening agent that requires an acidic ingredient in the
recipe (like buttermilk, yogurt, or lemon juice) to activate and produce carbon dioxide.
Baking powder, by contrast, already contains its own acid components alongside the
baking soda, which is why it can leaven a recipe on its own.

Because of this difference in strength, baking soda is roughly three to four times more
powerful per gram than baking powder. If a recipe calls for one teaspoon of baking soda
and you only have baking powder on hand, you'll typically need to use three to four
teaspoons of baking powder to get a comparable rise.

One side effect of this substitution is flavor: since you're adding several times more
powder, and baking powder has a distinct slightly metallic or chemical aftertaste at
high concentrations, the final result may taste noticeably different from the original
recipe, especially in delicate baked goods like sponge cakes.

Title: Freezing Cooked Rice Safely

Cooked rice carries a higher food-safety risk than most people realize, because raw rice
can contain spores of Bacillus cereus, a bacterium that survives cooking and can produce
toxins if the rice is left at room temperature too long afterward. To minimize this risk,
cooked rice should be cooled within one hour of cooking rather than left out to cool
gradually on the counter.

The fastest safe way to cool rice is to spread it in a thin, even layer on a baking
tray, which increases surface area and lets heat escape quickly, rather than leaving it
mounded in a pot. Once cooled, transfer it to airtight containers or freezer bags,
pressing out excess air, and freeze in portions you're likely to reheat all at once.

Frozen rice keeps at peak quality for about one month, though it remains safe to eat
well beyond that if it stays consistently frozen, with some quality loss in texture.

Title: The Maillard Reaction in Searing Meat

The Maillard reaction is a chemical process between amino acids and reducing sugars in
food, occurring most readily at temperatures above roughly 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
It's responsible for the deep brown crust and hundreds of new flavor and aroma compounds
that develop when meat is seared, bread is toasted, or coffee is roasted.

To get a good sear at home, pat the surface of the meat completely dry with paper towels
first, since surface moisture has to fully evaporate before browning can even begin. Use
a heavy pan preheated until visibly hot, and avoid overcrowding — too much food at once
drops the pan's temperature and traps steam, which cooks the surface instead of browning
it, no matter how good your technique otherwise is. Resting the meat for several minutes
after cooking allows redistributed juices to settle, improving texture when sliced.

Title: Reading a Nutrition Label Correctly

Standard nutrition labels list serving size first, since every number below it is
scaled to that amount rather than the whole package — a common misreading mistake.
Calories come next, followed by macronutrients (total fat, carbohydrates, protein) in
a fixed order, with micronutrients like sodium and specific vitamins listed further
down. The Percent Daily Value column is based on a generic 2,000-calorie diet and is
meant as a rough guideline, not a personalized target.

Manufacturers are legally permitted to round certain values — for example, anything
under 0.5 grams of trans fat per serving can be listed as "0g," which is why a product
advertising zero trans fat may still contain a small, cumulative amount if you eat
multiple servings.

Title: Understanding Food Expiration Dates vs. Best-By Dates

"Expiration" dates and "best-by" dates are regulated differently and mean different
things. A best-by date is a manufacturer's estimate of peak quality, not safety — food
is often still perfectly fine to eat after this date, especially shelf-stable items like
crackers or canned goods. A "use-by" or true expiration date, seen mostly on perishables
like deli meat or infant formula, is closer to an actual safety cutoff.

Manufacturers set these dates conservatively, factoring in storage conditions that
assume some temperature fluctuation, which is why food kept consistently refrigerated
often outlasts its printed date by a meaningful margin without any safety concern.

Title: How Grocery Store Loyalty Points Are Calculated

Most grocery loyalty programs award points based on pre-tax spending, typically one
point per dollar, with bonus multipliers on specific categories that rotate weekly or
monthly. Points usually expire after twelve to twenty-four months of account inactivity,
though this varies significantly by retailer.
